newsitem.title: USA: Small, young businesses shift the economic landscape.
newsitem.headline: Small, young businesses shift the economic landscape.

text.p: Small, young companies that sought growth regardless of the economic climate produced the most jobs in the United States over the past several years while large, older companies shrank, according to a new study.
That trend is likely to continue, creating opportunities for new businesses and jobs for the bulk of the new workers in the American economy.

The study by Cognetics Inc., a Cambridge, Mass.-based small business research group, confirmed the headlines that have become commonplace over the past few years -- big business is on balance cutting back jobs.

But it highlights a second element that the headlines may be missing -- that the lion's share of job growth over the past few years is coming from small, growing companies, regardless of the economy's overall strength.
The study could be instructive for small businesses in a number of ways.
First off, don't transpose grim headlines to your own business. If the economy is doing badly, it may actually be more advantageous for a small and nimble company.

Secondly, just because small companies have the fastest growth and create the bulk of new jobs, doesn't mean that a small business will automatically be part of that group -- indeed, the study says most small businesses don't grow. You have to aim for growth to become one of the economic engines.
The study clearly shows where job growth has originated over the past several years. Contrasting the smallest companies with the biggest over the period, the results are startling.

Companies with one to four workers created 3.8 million more jobs than they eliminated in 1991-1995, the study said. But the giants, companies with more than 5,000 workers, eliminated 3.4 million more jobs than they created.

The study points out that this occurred in a recovery period from the last recession, and is fairly typical. In hard economic times, small firms tend to dominate in growth. But even when the economy is expanding, they tend to outpace larger companies, creating two out of every three jobs, the study said.

Right now, the economy is split down the middle between those who work at large firms (those with more than 100 employees) and those at small firms (less than 100 workers). In 1991-1995, the bottom half created 68 percent of all new jobs, while the top half produced 32 percent. But including layoffs, the top half on balance lost jobs.
"In every industry group, smaller firms outgrew larger ones," the study said. "Small manufacturers grew by 9.9 percent, while larger ones shrank by 2.4 percent."

In fact, the study said, the decline in larger manufacturing companies actually was a boon for the smaller firms, "because poorly performing large firms open up lots of opportunity for smaller ones in the same sector."

The study said manufacturing was the second-slowest growing sector of the economy in 1991-1995. "Its larger firms declined, and its small ones grew faster than any other group in the economy," the study said.

But not all small companies grow -- just the ones that aim for it. These fast-growing firms accounted for 80 percent of the job growth, adding 6 million of the 7.7 million jobs that were created in the economy during 1991-1995.

They are found in all industries, roughly in the same proportion as the industry is to the overall economy. High technology represents less than 2 percent of these companies; the bulk of them are in the services industry, the study said.

Are all of these new jobs hamburger flippers or other low-wage positions? The study suggests not. Although small companies on average pay less than large firms, they tend to add jobs across the wage spectrum.

Large, expanding companies tend to pay higher wages but they are far more likely to lay off highly paid workers. Indeed, during the period of the study, high-wage jobs at large companies declined by 1.4 million while those at small firms expanded by 4.3 million.
